extracted.intended_audience: employers, industry stakeholders, state and federal rulemakers, and commenters on OSHA's heat standard NPRM
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and proposed regulatory provisions for an OSHA Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard, covering monitoring, rest breaks, water, acclimatization, training, written programs, controls, and protections for mobile or lone workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in monitoring methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The Panel recommends that OSHA allow flexibility in monitoring methods and not mandate a single method that employers must use to measure heat in their workplace or on their worksite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA's proposed standard provides flexibility in both what heat metric employers can use and how they are required to monitor the worksite (including allowing outdoor employers to use the forecast instead of on-site monitoring). The preamble notes that measurements with a WBGT can be complicated and difficult for some employers and that temperature can vary across indoor facilities or for mobile workers; therefore multiple monitoring options should be allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify how and when temperature monitoring must occur
rubrics_metrics.description: The Panel recommends that OSHA clarify how and when temperature monitoring must occur for all employers but especially for those with indoor settings and those with mobile workforces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders reported difficulties: spatial variability indoors, mobile workers visiting many locations in a day, and uncertainty about which areas must be routinely monitored. OSHA's proposal and explanation aim to provide guidance on monitoring frequency, locations to verify against triggers, and options to use forecasts/heat apps rather than continuous on-site measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest breaks: allow flexibility and clarify location/activities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Panel recommends allowing employers flexibility in the frequency of any rest breaks required and clarifying where workers can take breaks and what activities may be allowed during rest breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many SERs objected to prescriptive break frequency/duration; examples of concerns include inability to stop some processes (pouring concrete), PPE redonning time, working at heights, and preference for shaded outdoor breaks. OSHA's proposed standard: rest breaks required at the initial heat trigger when needed; under the high heat trigger a minimum 15-minute paid rest break is required every two hours, with a meal break allowed to count as a rest break. Proposed provisions specify requirements for indoor and outdoor break areas and allow employer choice among cooling options (e.g., shade OR air conditioning for outdoor breaks; air conditioning OR increased air movement and, if appropriate, de-humidification for indoor breaks). The preamble clarifies that no work activities would be allowed during rest breaks at the high heat trigger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of drinking water (including 'suitably cool' and amount)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must supply drinking water; Panel recommends eliminating or better defining 'suitably cool' and allow flexibility in how much water is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA is including the term 'suitably cool' (consistent with 29 CFR 1928.110 and California regs) to provide flexibility. The preamble cites evidence that cool/cold water is more palatable and encourages hydration. OSHA specifies the amount employers need to provide (guidance for complying with provision of 1 quart of cool water every hour) and states it is specifying the amount to provide, not the amount employees must drink. The Panel asked OSHA to clarify methods for complying and allow flexibility where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization provisions with multiple options
rubrics_metrics.description: The Panel recommends that OSHA provide multiple options for acclimatization in the rule to allow employers flexibility in determining the best method for acclimatizing their workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SER concerns include wage/payment impacts (workers quitting, paying minimum hours), inability to assign light-duty tasks, and belief that new hires may self-select or already be acclimatized. Employers also reported informal acclimatization practices (enhanced supervision, buddy systems, training process). OSHA preliminarily finds acclimatization effective and the proposed standard offers a gradual exposure option and an option to implement high heat trigger protections during an employee's first week of work. OSHA requests comments on acclimatization during heat waves, after illness, examples of existing programs, and the clarity of 'similar heat conditions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections and employer responsibilities for lone and mobile workers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Panel recommends that OSHA address unique situations of employers whose employees work alone and/or travel to many worksites each day and offer flexibility and clarification of employer responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SERs expressed concerns about monitoring temperatures for mobile workers, verifying which locations to monitor, ensuring breaks, and observing signs/symptoms for lone workers. OSHA proposes using Heat Index as the trigger metric (readily available via forecast or apps), clarifies employers do not need continuous monitoring but must verify whether temperatures exceed triggers, and proposes maintaining two-way communication with lone workers. When the high heat trigger is met or exceeded, the proposed standard would require employers to stay in contact at least every two hours with employees working alone. OSHA notes responsibilities for lone-worker safety are not unique to this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust training requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Training is an essential preventive step; the Panel recommends including a robust training provision and continuing support for employer training efforts through sample materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SERs reported providing training (formal and informal) on recognition of signs/symptoms, response, hydration, working pace, contacting supervisors for breaks/water, locations of cool down areas, sleep/rest, acclimatization, and medical treatment. OSHA preliminarily finds training necessary for employees to recognize hazards and understand workplace-specific controls and the proposed standard's requirements. OSHA expects to provide guidance, sample curriculum, videos, and other compliance assistance to help employers implement training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Program (HIIPP) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Require a HIIPP that allows employers flexibility to tailor plans to industry, location, and activities; consider an exemption for very small employers; require review and updates at least annually and after significant HRI events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SERs were largely supportive of a written plan but requested flexibility and a possible exemption for employers with 10 or fewer employees. OSHA proposes that employers with more than 10 employees must have a written HIIPP; employers with multiple substantially similar worksites may develop plans by work site type provided site-specific information is included. Employers with existing plans must incorporate missing required elements and train employees on updates. OSHA would require review and evaluation of the HIIPP whenever a heat-related injury or illness occurs that results in death, days away from work, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness, and at least annually, updating the HIIPP as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in engineering and administrative controls
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA and the Panel recommend allowing as much flexibility as possible for employers to implement feasible engineering and administrative controls appropriate to their workplace and activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SERs noted infeasibility of some controls: AC ineffective for very large buildings, fan placement limited by contamination risks, misting fans creating slipping hazards, portable shelters infeasible on roofs, and work-start time changes limited by local constraints. Employers reported using administrative controls (shift changes, reminders, buddy systems, electronic check-ins) and technologies (biometric monitors, urine color self-monitoring). OSHA drafted the rule to allow multiple engineering control options and employer choice to minimize feasibility problems while protecting workers.
